question: What happens to a collective agreement or arbitral award when a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which the Part applies?
answer:
**Successor Rights and Obligations**

**Application of Collective Agreements**

When a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which the Part applies, a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time of the deletion or severance continues in force, subject to certain conditions.

**Continuation of Collective Agreements**

According to Section 47.1 of the Canada Labour Code,
"...the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise..."

**Application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act**

The Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act also applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award.
"...the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a)..."

**Board's Determination**

The Board shall make an order determining whether the employees of the corporation or business who are bound by the collective agreement or arbitral award constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit.
"...the Board, by order, shall (a) determine whether the employees of the corporation or business who are bound by any collective agreement or arbitral award constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining; (b) determine which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit..."

**Effect on Collective Agreements**

The Board's determination shall also determine whether the collective agreement or arbitral award shall remain in force, and if so, whether it shall remain in force until the expiration of its term or expire on such earlier date as the Board may fix.
"...whether the employees of the corporation or business who are bound by any collective agreement or arbitral award constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining; (b) determine which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit; and (c) in respect of each collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to employees of the corporation or business, (i) determine whether the collective agreement or arbitral award shall remain in force, and (ii) if the collective agreement or arbitral award is to remain in force, determine whether it shall remain in force until the expiration of its term or expire on such earlier date as the Board may fix."

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-14_18", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "What we heard: Modernizing federal labour standards", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "CONTRACT RETENDERING Currently, when the employees of an original contractor are rehired by a new contactor to do the same work, their employment generally does not have to be treated as continuous and any entitlements or benefits that are tied to the length of their employment can be lost.  We heard from unions and labour organizations that in some sectors, contract retendering is not used to achieve legitimate efficiencies, but rather as a way to undermine seniority entitlements and substitute a cheaper, non-union contractor for a unionized one. They told us that abusive practices of contract retendering, or “contract flipping”, are a serious issue at airports. One union mentioned the situation in the school bus industry (of which many of the larger employers fall under federal jurisdiction), where school boards secure school bus services through a competitive bidding system. There was concern that the intensification of contracting out has meant that service providers have to compete based on how little they can pay their workforce instead of how well they do the job.  “When contracts flip, workers lose any wage gains and benefits they have earned over their years of service. They must reapply for work and start over at minimum wage. This is not only disruptive to the lives of workers, it disrupts workplace continuity.” Unite here Local 40, written submission, January 2018  Four unions suggested ensuring “successor rights” for employees in cases where the same or similar services are offered following contract retendering. More specifically, they recommended that section 189 in Part III of the Code be amended to ensure that wages and access to seniority entitlements are treated as continuous when a new contract is awarded and jobs are transferred from one service provider to another. They also recommended extending equal remuneration protection in Part I of the Code (section 47.3) beyond pre-board security screening services to apply to any third-party service contractor.  « The FTQ suggests that the Code include a presumption of continuous service in cases of successive fixed term employment contracts and recurring temporary employment. This presumption should also apply in the case of business succession in order to preserve the rights associated with length of service: the new business should therefore be bound by the length of service and thus by the rights acquired under its predecessor » FTQ, written submission, January 2018"

SUBJECT Application of the Federal Contractors Program (FCP) requirements applicable to dual jurisdiction employers who are bidding on contracts issued by Canada.  2. ISSUE This guideline provides direction on whether an organization that is subject to the Legislated Employment Equity Program (LEEP) can also be subject to the FCP in the event that a portion of its workforce is provincially regulated.  3. BACKGROUND The LEEP covers federally-regulated private sector  employers, Crown corporations and other federal organizations that have at  least 100 or more employees and are subject to the Employment Equity Act (the Act). LEEP’s mandate is to promote,  support and enhance employment equity for four designated groups: women,  Aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and members of visible  minorities. Employers that are subject to the LEEP have certain  obligations and responsibilities under the Act.   These employers are obligated to implement and report annually on  employment equity to the Labour Program and are subject to audits conducted by  the Canadian Human Rights Commission. The FCP targets provincially-regulated contractors with a  resident workforce in Canada of at least 100 or more permanent full-time and/or  permanent part-time employees who have received a federal contract for goods  and/or services that has a value of at least $1M or more. The FCP requires that  contractors make all reasonable efforts to implement employment equity so that  reasonable progress is made towards having full representation of the four  designated groups within their workforce. Compliance assessments are conducted  by the Labour Program one year after a contractor has been awarded a first  contract valued at $1M or more. Subsequent assessments may also be conducted  after three years. When it is determined that a contractor does not meet  his/her obligations under the FCP, the contractor loses the right to bid on  federal government goods and services contracts, standing offers or supply  arrangements of any value. In order to be reinstated to the FCP, a contractor  must implement employment equity in its workplace, inform the FCP of the  implementation, and be found in compliance through a compliance assessment."

question: What are the requirements for an employer who takes over providing services from a previous contractor under a contract or arrangement?
answer:
**Federal Contractors Program Requirements**

The Federal Contractors Program (FCP) requires that contractors make all reasonable efforts to implement employment equity, with the goal of achieving "reasonable progress" towards having full representation of the four designated groups within their workforce.
"FCP requires that  contractors make all reasonable efforts to implement employment equity so that  reasonable progress is made towards having full representation of the four  designated groups within their workforce."

**Successor Rights Under the Canada Labour Code**

The Canada Labour Code also provides for successor rights under section 189, which ensures that wages and access to seniority entitlements are treated as continuous when a new contract is awarded and jobs are transferred from one service provider to another.
"...section 189 in Part III of the Code be amended to ensure that wages and access to seniority entitlements are treated as continuous when a new contract is awarded and jobs are transferred from one service provider to another."

**Equal Remuneration Protection**

The Canada Labour Code also provides for equal remuneration protection under section 47.3, which requires that an employer who succeeds a previous contractor as the provider of services must pay to the employees providing the services under that contract or arrangement
"...remuneration not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied."
"An employer who succeeds a previous contractor as the provider of services, in accordance with a contract or other arrangement, must pay to the employees providing the services under that contract or arrangement remuneration not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied."

**Contract Flipping and Successor Rights**

The Canada Labour Code also addresses the issue of contract flipping, where a service provider is replaced by another provider without providing continuity of employment to the workers. This is considered a serious issue and can result in the loss of seniority entitlements and benefits.
"...contracts flip, workers lose any wage gains and benefits they have earned over their years of service. They must reapply for work and start over at minimum wage."

The Canada Labour Code also provides for regulations and compliance assessments to ensure that employers are meeting the requirements for successor rights and equal remuneration protection.

question: What can a certified bargaining agent or an employer do to initiate collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force?
answer:
**Initiating Collective Bargaining**

**Certified Bargaining Agent's Options**

A certified bargaining agent may
"...require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement." This quote highlights the bargaining agent's initiative to start collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force.

**Employer's Options**

An employer may also
"...require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement." This quote emphasizes the employer's role in initiating collective bargaining, highlighting the bargaining agent's responsibility to start negotiations.

**Notice to Bargain**

A certified bargaining agent or an employer may give notice to bargain, as stated in Section 48 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

**Designation of Employers' Organization**

In certain industries, an employers' organization may be designated as the employer, as stated in Section 33 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

**Initiating Collective Bargaining**

In all cases, a certified bargaining agent or an employer may initiate collective bargaining by giving notice to bargain, as stated in Section 48 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

question: What are the requirements for a party to a collective agreement to initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing, revising, or entering into a new collective agreement?
answer:
**Initiating Collective Bargaining for a New Collective Agreement**

**Timeframe for Initiating Collective Bargaining**

A party to a collective agreement may initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a new collective agreement
"...within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement..." This timeframe is specified in Section 49 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Notice Requirement**

A party to a collective agreement must give notice to the other party requiring them to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement. This notice must be given
"...within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement..." This notice requirement is specified in Section 49 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Duty to Bargain and Not to Change Terms and Conditions**

A party to a collective agreement must also comply with the duty to bargain and not to change terms and conditions. This duty is specified in Section 50 of the Canada Labour Code, which states that
"...the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..."

**Effect of Failing to Initiate Collective Bargaining**

Failing to initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing, revising, or entering into a new collective agreement may result in the expiration of the collective agreement. This is specified in Section 49 of the Canada Labour Code, which states that
"...where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and no trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, an application by a trade union for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit may be made at any time..."

**Notice to Bargain**

A party to a collective agreement must also give notice to the other party requiring them to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement. This notice must be given
"...within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement..." This notice requirement is specified in Section 49 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Duty to Bargain and Not to Change Terms and Conditions**

A party to a collective agreement must also comply with the duty to bargain and not to change terms and conditions. This duty is specified in Section 50 of the Canada Labour Code, which states that
"...the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..."

question: What are the obligations of the bargaining agent and the employer once notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
answer:
**Obligations of the Bargaining Agent and the Employer**

**Section 50: Duty to Bargain and Not to Change Terms and Conditions**

Where notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part,
"...the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..."

This quote highlights the immediate obligation of the bargaining agent and the employer to meet and commence collective bargaining. The employer is also required to make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement.

**Section 48: Notice to Bargain to Enter into a Collective Agreement**

Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement.

This quote emphasizes the importance of the bargaining agent and the employer initiating collective bargaining once notice has been given. The employer is also given the option to require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining.

**Section 49: Notice to Bargain to Renew or Revise a Collective Agreement or Enter a New Collective Agreement**

Either party to a collective agreement may, within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement, by notice, require the other party to the collective agreement to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement.

This quote highlights the obligation of the bargaining agent and the employer to initiate collective bargaining once the term of the collective agreement has expired or is set to expire. The employer is also given the option to require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining.

**Section 36: Effect of Certification**

Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit,
"(a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

This quote emphasizes the exclusive authority of the bargaining agent to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit. This authority is crucial in ensuring that the bargaining agent and the employer initiate collective bargaining once notice has been given.

**Section 51: Definition of Technological Change**

"...the introduction by an employer into their work, undertaking or business of equipment or material of a different nature or kind than that previously utilized by the employer in the operation of the work, undertaking or business; and (b) a change in the manner in which the employer carries on the work, undertaking or business that is directly related to the introduction of that equipment or material."

**Section 51(2): Exemption from Sections 52, 54, and 55
"Sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, in respect of a technological change, to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement where (a) the employer has given to the bargaining agent a notice in writing of the technological change that is substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2), (i) prior to the day on which the employer and the bargaining agent entered into the collective agreement, if the notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into that collective agreement was given pursuant to section 48, or (ii) not later than the last day on which notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the collective agreement could have been given pursuant to subsection 49(1), if the notice was given under that subsection..."

**Section 51(2)(b): Collective Agreement Provisions
"(b) the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement..."

**Section 51(2)(c): Collective Agreement Provisions
"...or (c) the collective agreement contains provisions that (i) are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and (ii) specify that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent."

**Section 54: Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain
"...the Board may, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection..."

question: What are the requirements for an employer bound by a collective agreement to implement a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees?
answer:
**Requirements for Technological Change**

**Section 52: Notice of Technological Change**

An employer who is bound by a collective agreement and who proposes to effect a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of the employer's employees to whom the collective agreement applies shall give notice of the technological change to the bargaining agent bound by the collective agreement at least one hundred and twenty days prior to the date on which the technological change is to be effected.

**Section 52: Contents of Notice**

The notice referred to in subsection (1) shall be in writing and shall state (a) the nature of the technological change; (b) the date on which the employer proposes to effect the technological change; (c) the approximate number and type of employees likely to be affected by the technological change; (d) the effect that the technological change is likely to have on the terms and conditions or security of employment of the employees affected; and (e) such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4).

**Section 51: Application of Sections 52 to 55**

Sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, in respect of a technological change, to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement where (a) the employer has given to the bargaining agent a notice in writing of the technological change that is substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2), (i) prior to the day on which the employer and the bargaining agent entered into the collective agreement, if the notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into that collective agreement was given pursuant to section 48, or (ii) not later than the last day on which notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the collective agreement could have been given pursuant to subsection 49(1), if the notice was given under that subsection; (b) the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement; or (c) the collective agreement contains provisions that (i) are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and (ii) specify that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent.

**Section 53: Application for Order Respecting Technological Change**

Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged.

question: What can a bargaining agent do if they allege that an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes, and what are the potential outcomes of such an action?
answer:
**Application for Order**

A bargaining agent who alleges that an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes can apply to the Board for an order determining the matters alleged under subsection 53(1).
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."

**Potential Outcomes**

The Board may, by order, determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change, or determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change.
"An order of the Board made under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of an employer is deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, and the Board shall concurrently, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1)."

**Direction to Employer**

The Board may also direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for a specified period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate.
"The Board may, in any order made under paragraph (2)(b), or by order made after consultation with the parties pending the making of any order under subsection (2), (a) direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate..."

**Reinstatement of Employees**

The Board may also require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change.
"...require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change..."

**Reimbursement of Loss of Pay**

The Board may also require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement.
"...require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement."

question: What recourse does a bargaining agent have when it receives notice of a technological change that may adversely affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees bound by a collective agreement?
answer:
**Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain**

A bargaining agent has the recourse to apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining, as stated in Section 54 of the Canada Labour Code.
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."

**Granting Leave to Serve Notice to Bargain**

The Board may grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining, as stated in Section 54 of the Canada Labour Code.
"Where the Board has received from a bargaining agent an application for an order under subsection (1), and it is satisfied that the technological change in respect of which the bargaining agent has received notice given pursuant to section 52 is likely, substantially and adversely, to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees to whom the collective agreement between the bargaining agent and the employer applies, the Board may, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection (1)."

**Effect of the Order**

The order granted by the Board has the effect of directing the employer not to proceed with the technological change, as stated in Section 55 of the Canada Labour Code.
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."

**Reinstatement of Employees**

The order granted by the Board may also require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change, as stated in Section 55 of the Canada Labour Code.
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."

**Effect on the Employer**

The order granted by the Board has the effect of directing the employer not to proceed with the technological change, as stated in Section 55 of the Canada Labour Code.
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."

question: What happens to an employer's ability to effect a technological change when a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1)?
answer:
**Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain**

When a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer's ability to effect a technological change is "limited by the order of the Board".


**Limitation of Technological Change**

The Board may, by order,
"...direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate..."


**Effect on Employer's Ability to Effect Technological Change**

This limitation applies to the employer's ability to effect a technological change, as the Board may grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1).


**Consequence of Board's Order**

The Board's order may also require the employer to
"...any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change..." and to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement.


**Deemed Notice of Technological Change**

The Board's order is deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, which gives the bargaining agent the right to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1).

question: Who is bound by a collective agreement entered into between a bargaining agent and an employer in respect of a bargaining unit?
answer:
**Who is Bound by a Collective Agreement?**

**Section 56: Effect of Collective Agreement**

A collective agreement entered into between a bargaining agent and an employer in respect of a bargaining unit is, subject to and for the purposes of this Part, binding on the bargaining agent, every employee in the bargaining unit and the employer.

**Section 33: Designation of Employers' Organization**

Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers' organization, the Board may designate the employers' organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers' organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers' organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part.

**Section 33: Designation of Employers' Organization (Continued)**

The Board may, on application by the employers' organization, include in the designation referred to in subsection (1) any employer that becomes a member of the employers' organization if it is satisfied that that employer has granted appropriate authority to the employers' organization to enable the employers' organization to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer and that such an inclusion would ensure the fulfilment of the objectives of this Part.

**Section 33: Designation of Employers' Organization (Effect on Binding)**

Where the Board designates an employers' organization as an employer pursuant to subsection (1), (a) the employers' organization and each employer forming the employers' organization is bound by any collective agreement entered into by the employers' organization and the trade union concerned; and (b) this Part applies, except as otherwise provided, as if the employers' organization were an employer.

**Content and Interpretation of Collective Agreements**

**Resolution of Differences
"Every collective agreement shall contain a provision for final settlement without stoppage of work, by arbitration or otherwise, of all differences between the parties to or employees bound by the collective agreement, concerning its interpretation, application, administration or alleged contravention."
"Every collective agreement shall contain a provision for final settlement without stoppage of work, by arbitration or otherwise, of all differences between the parties to or employees bound by the collective agreement, concerning its interpretation, application, administration or alleged contravention."

This provision is required to be included in a collective agreement in Canada regarding the resolution of differences between parties.

**Arbitration Board Selection
"Where a difference described in subsection 57(1) is submitted to an arbitration board, the decision of a majority of those comprising the board is the decision of the board, but if a majority of those comprising the board cannot agree on a decision, the decision of the chairperson of the board is the decision of the board."
"Where a difference described in subsection 57(1) is submitted to an arbitration board, the decision of a majority of those comprising the board is the decision of the board, but if a majority of those comprising the board cannot agree on a decision, the decision of the chairperson of the board is the decision of the board."

This quote highlights the importance of a majority decision in an arbitration board, as well as the role of the chairperson in case of a tie.

**Selection of Arbitrator or Arbitration Board Chairperson
"Where a collective agreement provides for final settlement, without stoppage of work, of differences described in subsection (1) by an arbitrator or arbitration board and the parties or their nominees are unable to agree on the selection of an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, as the case may be, either party or its nominee may, notwithstanding anything in the collective agreement, make a written request to the Minister to appoint an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, as the case may be."

**Procedure for Making a Decision**

The arbitration board makes a decision by a majority vote, unless the board is unable to agree, in which case the chairperson's decision is considered the decision of the board. This procedure ensures that the decision is made in a fair and impartial manner.

question: What happens when a question arises regarding the existence of a collective agreement or the identification of parties bound by it during an arbitration proceeding, and how does it affect the proceeding?
answer:
**Understanding the Process**

When a question arises regarding the existence of a collective agreement or the identification of parties bound by it during an arbitration proceeding, the arbitrator or arbitration board, the Minister, or any alleged party may refer the question to the Board for determination.

**Section 65: Referral of Questions**

According to Section 65 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where any question arises in connection with a matter that has been referred to an arbitrator or arbitration board, relating to the existence of a collective agreement or the identification of the parties or employees bound by a collective agreement, the arbitrator or arbitration board, the Minister or any alleged party may refer the question to the Board for determination."

**Effect on the Proceeding**

The referral of a question to the Board may suspend the proceeding, as stated in Section 65:
"The referral of any question to the Board pursuant to subsection (1) shall not operate to suspend any proceeding before an arbitrator or arbitration board unless the arbitrator or arbitration board decides that the nature of the question warrants a suspension of the proceeding or the Board directs the suspension of the proceeding."

**Arbitration Board's Discretion**

The arbitration board has the discretion to decide whether to suspend the proceeding or not. As stated in Section 64,
"The failure of an arbitrator or arbitration board to make or give any order or decision within the sixty days referred to in subsection (1) does not affect the jurisdiction of the arbitrator or arbitration board to continue with and complete the arbitration proceedings..."

**No Suspension by Default**

The arbitration board's failure to make a decision within the specified time frame does not automatically suspend the proceeding. Instead, the board has the discretion to decide whether to suspend the proceeding or not. This means that the proceeding may continue, even if the board does not make a decision within the specified time frame.

**Implications of a Collective Agreement with No Term Provision**

A collective agreement that contains no provision as to its term or is for a term of less than one year

The Board has the power to alter the term of a collective agreement, but only in certain circumstances. This means that the Board can review the term of the collective agreement and make changes as needed, but only in specific circumstances.

**Limitations on Altering the Term of a Collective Agreement**

It is worth noting that the term of a collective agreement cannot be altered or revised during its initial term. (CLC-67, Section 67(4)) This means that the parties involved must agree to a revision of the term before the expiration of the initial term, and must obtain approval from the Board before making any changes. The Board may grant approval, but only if the parties involved meet certain requirements and follow the proper procedures.

question: What are the obligations of a trade union when referring persons to employment pursuant to a collective agreement?
answer:
**Obligations of a Trade Union**

**Establishing Rules for Referrals**

A trade union engaged in the referral of persons to employment pursuant to a collective agreement
"...shall establish rules for the purpose of making such referrals and apply those rules fairly and without discrimination." This quote highlights the importance of the trade union's role in ensuring that the referral process is fair and non-discriminatory.

**Posting Rules for Fairness**

The trade union's rules for referrals must be kept
"...posted in a conspicuous place in every area of premises occupied by the trade union in which persons seeking referral normally gather." This requirement ensures that the trade union's rules are readily available and accessible to those seeking employment, promoting transparency and fairness in the referral process.

**Fairness and Non-Discrimination**

The trade union's rules must be applied "fairly and without discrimination." This quote emphasizes the need for the trade union to treat all individuals seeking employment with equal respect and dignity, regardless of their background or circumstances.

**Responsibility for Fair Practices**

The trade union's rules and practices are subject to inspection by any person employed by the trade union who has been referred to employment by the trade union. This quote highlights the trade union's responsibility to ensure that its rules and practices are fair and non-discriminatory, and that individuals seeking employment are treated with respect and dignity.

**Application of Rules**

The trade union's rules must be applied in a fair and non-discriminatory manner to all persons seeking referral. This quote emphasizes the importance of the trade union's commitment to fairness and non-discrimination in its referral practices.

**Consequences of Non-Compliance**

The trade union's failure to establish and apply rules for referrals fairly and without discrimination may result in the certification of a bargaining agent other than the trade union. This quote highlights the potential consequences of the trade union's non-compliance with its obligations, emphasizing the importance of its commitment to fairness and non-discrimination in its referral practices.

question: What happens when a trade union requests that union dues be deducted from the wages of employees in a bargaining unit, and are there any exceptions for employees who object to paying these dues?
answer:
**Request for Union Dues Deduction**

**Section 70 of the Canada Labour Code
"Where a trade union that is the bargaining agent for employees in a bargaining unit so requests, there shall be included in the collective agreement between the trade union and the employer of the employees a provision requiring the employer to deduct from the wages of each employee in the unit affected by the collective agreement, whether or not the employee is a member of the union, the amount of the regular union dues..."

This section outlines the process for a trade union to request that union dues be deducted from the wages of employees in a bargaining unit. The provision requires the employer to deduct the union dues from the wages of each employee, whether or not the employee is a member of the union.

**Exceptions for Employees Objecting to Union Dues**

**Section 70 of the Canada Labour Code
"Where the Board is satisfied that an employee, because of their religious conviction or beliefs, objects to joining a trade union or to paying regular union dues to a trade union, the Board may order that the provision in a collective agreement requiring, as a condition of employment, membership in a trade union or requiring the payment of regular union dues to a trade union does not apply to that employee so long as an amount equal to the amount of the regular union dues is paid by the employee, either directly or by way of deduction from their wages, to a registered charity mutually agreed on by the employee and the trade union."

This section provides an exception for employees who object to paying union dues due to religious convictions or beliefs. The Board may order that the provision in the collective agreement requiring membership in the trade union or payment of union dues does not apply to the employee, as long as the employee pays an amount equal to the union dues to a registered charity.

question: What steps must be taken by a party to a collective bargaining agreement when they are unable to reach an agreement or when collective bargaining has not commenced within the required timeframe?
answer:
**Notice of Dispute**

When a party to a collective bargaining agreement is unable to reach an agreement or when collective bargaining has not commenced within the required timeframe, they must inform the Minister of their failure to enter into, renew or revise a collective agreement. This is stated in Section 71(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where a notice to commence collective bargaining has been given under this Part, either party may inform the Minister, by sending a notice of dispute, of their failure to enter into, renew or revise a collective agreement where (a) collective bargaining has not commenced within the time fixed by this Part; or (b) the parties have bargained collectively for the purpose of entering into or revising a collective agreement but have been unable to reach agreement."

**Conciliation Procedures**

The party must send a notice of dispute to the Minister, who will then take steps to assist the parties in reaching an agreement. This notice must be sent within the required timeframe, as stated in Section 71(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

**Board Involvement**

If the parties are unable to reach an agreement, the Minister may refer the dispute to the Board, which will then attempt to assist the parties in reaching an agreement. This is stated in Section 71(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where a notice of dispute has been given under subsection (1), the Minister shall, without delay, refer the dispute to the Board."

**Notice to Bargain**

In addition to sending a notice of dispute, the party must also give notice to bargain to the other party, as stated in Section 48 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

**Duty to Bargain**

The party must also give notice to bargain to the other party, as stated in Section 50 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part, (a) the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..."

**Effect of Certification**

The party must also give notice to bargain to the other party, as stated in Section 36 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where a trade union is certified as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit, (a) the trade union so certified has exclusive authority to bargain collectively on behalf of the employees in the bargaining unit..."

**Consequences of Failure to Bargain**

If the parties are unable to reach an agreement or if collective bargaining has not commenced within the required timeframe, the Minister may take steps to assist the parties in reaching an agreement. This is stated in Section 71(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"Where a notice of dispute has been given under subsection (1), the Minister shall, without delay, refer the dispute to the Board."

question: What are the possible actions the Minister can take upon receiving a notice or considering it necessary to assist parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement?
answer:
**Minister's Actions Upon Receiving a Notice**

The Minister has the authority to take several actions upon receiving a notice or considering it necessary to assist parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement.

**Appointing a Conciliation Officer**

The Minister may "appoint a conciliation officer" (CLC-72(1)(a)) to assist the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement. This officer shall
"...forthwith after the appointment, confer with the parties to the dispute and endeavour to assist them in entering into or revising a collective agreement..."(a)).

**Appointing a Conciliation Commissioner**

Alternatively, the Minister may "appoint a conciliation commissioner" (CLC-72(1)(b)) to take on this role. The conciliation commissioner shall also
"...forthwith after the appointment, confer with the parties to the dispute and endeavour to assist them in entering into or revising a collective agreement..."(a)).

**Establishing a Conciliation Board**

In some cases, the Minister may establish a "conciliation board" (CLC-72(1)(c)) to assist the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement. The board shall
"...immediately endeavour to assist the parties to the dispute in entering into or revising a collective agreement..."(a)).

**Notifying Parties of Minister's Intention**

If the Minister does not receive a notice under section 71, but considers it advisable to take action, the Minister may
"...notify the parties, in writing, of the Minister’s intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner or establish a conciliation board." This notification informs the parties of the Minister's decision not to take action.

**Delivery of Notice to Conciliation Officer**

The Minister shall
"...deliver to the officer a copy of the notice given under section 71..." This delivery of the notice ensures that the conciliation officer is aware of the dispute and can begin working to assist the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement.

question: What is the primary role of a conciliation officer appointed during a labour dispute under the Canada Labour Code, and what are their key responsibilities?
answer:
**Conciliation Officer Role and Responsibilities**

**Primary Role of a Conciliation Officer**

The primary role of a conciliation officer appointed during a labour dispute under the Canada Labour Code is to
"...harmonious relations between trade unions and employers by assisting them in the negotiation of collective agreements and their renewal and the management of the relations resulting from the implementation of the agreements."

**Key Responsibilities of a Conciliation Officer**

A conciliation officer appointed under the Canada Labour Code is responsible for
"...forthwith after the appointment, confer with the parties to the dispute and endeavour to assist them in entering into or revising a collective agreement..."(a)). This responsibility is crucial in resolving labour disputes and promoting harmonious relations between trade unions and employers.

**Duties of a Conciliation Officer**

A conciliation officer appointed under the Canada Labour Code is also responsible for
"...within fourteen days after the date of the appointment or within the longer period that may be agreed to by the parties or allowed by the Minister, report to the Minister as to whether or not the officer has succeeded in assisting the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement."(b)). This duty ensures that the conciliation officer's efforts to resolve the labour dispute are tracked and reported to the Minister.

**Delivery of Notice to Conciliation Officer**

When a conciliation officer is appointed, the Minister shall
"...forthwith deliver to the officer a copy of the notice given under section 71 in respect of the dispute." This delivery of notice is essential in informing the conciliation officer of the labour dispute and enabling them to take on their key responsibilities.

**Mediation and Conciliation**

A conciliation officer appointed under the Canada Labour Code may also be involved in mediation and conciliation efforts. For example, the Minister may "refer other questions to them" (CLC-74(1)), indicating that the conciliation officer's role is not limited to resolving labour disputes through collective agreement negotiations. Instead, they may be involved in broader mediation and conciliation efforts to promote harmonious relations between trade unions and employers.

question: What are the primary duties of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board when appointed or established to resolve a labor dispute?
answer:
**Primary Duties of a Conciliation Commissioner or a Conciliation Board**

**Establishment and Appointment**

When a conciliation commissioner has been appointed or a conciliation board has been established, the Minister
"...must immediately deliver to the conciliation commissioner or the members of the conciliation board a copy of the notice of dispute sent under section 71..." This quote highlights the importance of the Minister's role in delivering the notice to the conciliation commissioner or board, ensuring that they are aware of the dispute and can begin their duties.

**Duties of a Conciliation Commissioner or a Conciliation Board**

A conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board shall
"...immediately endeavour to assist the parties to the dispute in entering into or revising a collective agreement..." This quote emphasizes the primary duty of a conciliation commissioner or board to assist the parties in reaching a collective agreement. This duty is further emphasized in subsection 72(1), which states that the Minister shall establish a conciliation board "where the Minister is of the opinion that the parties to the dispute are unwilling to enter into collective agreements on their own initiative."

**Report Requirements**

A conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board shall also submit a report to the Minister within fourteen days of their appointment or establishment. This report shall include the commissioner's or board's success or failure in assisting the parties to the dispute, as well as their findings and recommendations. This quote highlights the importance of transparency and accountability in the conciliation process, ensuring that the Minister is informed of the commissioner's or board's progress and outcomes.

**Time Limits and Procedure**

A conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may determine their own procedure, as stated in subsection 84(1) of the Canada Labour Code. This quote emphasizes the flexibility and autonomy of conciliation commissioners and boards in resolving labor disputes. However, they must also adhere to time limits and procedural requirements, as stated in subsection 74(2) of the Canada Labour Code. This quote highlights the importance of efficiency and effectiveness in the conciliation process, ensuring that disputes are resolved in a timely and orderly manner.

answer:
**Time Limits and Implications**

**Section 75: Time Limits**

The Minister may not extend the time for a conciliation officer to report, or for a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to submit a report, beyond sixty days after the date of appointment or establishment.
"Except with the consent of the parties, the Minister may not extend the time for a conciliation officer to report, or for a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to submit a report, beyond sixty days after the date of appointment or establishment."

This quote highlights the strict time limit for conciliation officers, commissioners, and boards to submit their reports. If they fail to do so within this timeframe, it does not invalidate the proceeding or terminate the authority of the conciliation officer, commissioner, or board.

**Section 113: Late Report Not Invalid
"The failure of a conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to report to the Minister within a period limited by this Part does not invalidate the proceeding or terminate the authority of the conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board."

This quote emphasizes that the failure to submit a report within the specified time limit does not have any negative consequences on the proceeding or the authority of the conciliation officer, commissioner, or board. This means that the proceeding can continue, and the authority of the conciliation officer, commissioner, or board remains intact.

**Exceptions to the Rule**

The quote from Section 75 also mentions an exception to the rule, where the parties consent to an extension of the time limit.
"Except with the consent of the parties, the Minister may not extend the time for a conciliation officer to report, or for a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to submit a report, beyond sixty days after the date of appointment or establishment."

This exception highlights that there are specific circumstances where the time limit can be extended, but only with the consent of the parties involved. This exception is important to note, as it provides a loophole for parties to agree to an extension of the time limit, which can have significant implications for the proceeding.

question: What happens when an employer and a bargaining agent agree to refer a matter related to a collective agreement to a third-party for determination?
answer:
**Agreement to Refer Matters to a Third-Party**

When an employer and a bargaining agent agree to refer a matter related to a collective agreement to a third-party for determination, they can do so "despite any other provision of this Part" (CLC-79(1)). This means that they can bypass the usual procedures and rules governing collective agreements and instead rely on a third-party to make a final and binding determination.

**Effect on the Right to Strike or Lockout**

By agreeing to refer matters to a third-party, the employer and the bargaining agent are effectively suspending their right to strike or lockout (CLC-79(2)). This is because they are undertaking to implement the determination made by the third-party, which means that they are committing to follow the decision of the third-party.

**Constitution of an Undertaking**

The agreement to refer matters to a third-party constitutes an undertaking to implement the determination (CLC-79(2)). This means that the employer and the bargaining agent are making a commitment to follow the decision of the third-party, which can have significant implications for the collective agreement and the relationship between the parties.

**Final and Binding Determination**

The determination made by the third-party is final and binding (CLC-79(1)). This means that the parties are required to comply with the decision of the third-party, which can help to resolve disputes and prevent strikes or lockouts.

**No Suspension of Proceedings**

It is worth noting that the referral of matters to a third-party does not automatically suspend proceedings before an arbitrator or arbitration board (CLC-65(2)). However, the arbitrator or arbitration board may decide to suspend the proceeding if it determines that the nature of the question warrants a suspension of the proceeding.

question: What happens if an employer and a bargaining agent fail to enter into a first collective agreement after being required to commence collective bargaining, and the Minister considers it necessary or advisable to intervene?
answer:
**Procedure for Minister Intervention**

**Notice of Dispute**

If an employer and a bargaining agent fail to enter into a first collective agreement after being required to commence collective bargaining, they must inform the Minister of their failure to enter into a collective agreement. The Minister must receive a notice of dispute within 15 days of the notice to commence collective bargaining being given.
"Where an employer or a bargaining agent is required, by notice given under section 48, to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the first collective agreement between the parties with respect to the bargaining unit for which the bargaining agent has been certified and the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have otherwise been met, the Minister may, if the Minister considers it necessary or advisable, at any time thereafter direct the Board to inquire into the dispute and, if the Board considers it advisable, to settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement between the parties."

**Minister's Intervention**

The Minister may direct the Board to inquire into the dispute and settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement between the parties. The Board shall proceed as directed by the Minister and shall give the parties an opportunity to present evidence and make representations. The Board may take into account the extent to which the parties have, or have not, bargained in good faith in an attempt to enter into the first collective agreement between them.
"In settling the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement under this section, the Board shall give the parties an opportunity to present evidence and make representations and the Board may take into account (a) the extent to which the parties have, or have not, bargained in good faith in an attempt to enter into the first collective agreement between them..."

**Effect of Minister's Intervention**

The Board's settlement of the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement shall constitute the collective agreement between the parties and shall be binding on them and on the employees in the bargaining unit, except to the extent that such terms and conditions are subsequently amended by the parties by agreement in writing. The agreement shall be effective for a period of two years after the date on which the Board settles the terms and conditions of the collective agreement.

question: What is the process for establishing a conciliation board under the Canada Labour Code, and who is responsible for appointing its members?
answer:
**Establishment of Conciliation Boards**

**Process for Establishing a Conciliation Board**

The process for establishing a conciliation board under the Canada Labour Code involves several steps. According to Section 82 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where the Minister has, pursuant to section 72, decided to establish a conciliation board, the Minister shall immediately, by notice in writing, require each of the parties to the dispute to nominate, within seven days after receipt by the party of the notice, one person to be a member of the conciliation board and, on receipt of the nomination within those seven days, the Minister shall appoint the nominee to be a member of the conciliation board."

This quote highlights the role of the Minister in initiating the establishment of a conciliation board. The Minister is responsible for deciding to establish a conciliation board and for requiring the parties to the dispute to nominate members.

**Appointment of Members**

The appointment of members to a conciliation board is a collaborative process between the Minister and the parties to the dispute. According to Section 82 of the Canada Labour Code,
"The members of a conciliation board appointed under subsection (1) or (2) shall, within five days after the appointment of the second member, nominate a third person, who is willing and ready to act, to be a member and chairperson of the conciliation board, and the Minister shall appoint that person to be a member and chairperson of the conciliation board."

This quote emphasizes the importance of collaboration between the Minister and the parties to the dispute in appointing members to a conciliation board. The Minister is responsible for appointing the third member and chairperson, while the parties to the dispute are responsible for nominating the second member.

**Responsibility for Appointing Members**

The responsibility for appointing members to a conciliation board is shared between the Minister and the parties to the dispute. The Minister is responsible for initiating the establishment of a conciliation board and for appointing the third member and chairperson, while the parties to the dispute are responsible for nominating members. According to Section 82 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where a person ceases to be a member of a conciliation board before the board has completed its work, another member shall be nominated and appointed in their place in accordance with section 82."

question: What are the requirements for a trade union or an employer to give notice of a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Notice Requirements**

The Canada Labour Code sets out the requirements for a trade union or an employer to give notice of a strike or lockout.

**Section 87.1: Definitions**

The Code defines the terms "employer" and "trade union" to include an employers' organization and a council of trade unions, respectively.
"employer includes an employers’ organization."
"...trade union trade union includes a council of trade unions."

**Section 87.2: Strike Notice**

A trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister.
"Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

**Section 87.2: Lockout Notice**

An employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister.
"Unless a strike not prohibited by this Part has occurred, an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

**Section 87.2: New Notice
"Unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, where no strike or lockout occurs on the date indicated in a notice given pursuant to subsection (1) or (2), a new notice of at least seventy-two hours must be given by the trade union or the employer if they wish to initiate a strike or lockout."
"Unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, where no strike or lockout occurs on the date indicated in a notice given pursuant to subsection (1) or (2), a new notice of at least seventy-two hours must be given by the trade union or the employer if they wish to initiate a strike or lockout."

**Section 87.2: Secret Ballot - Strike Vote**

A trade union must hold a secret ballot vote among the employees in the unit and receive the approval of the majority of the employees who voted, unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred.
"Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union may not declare or authorize a strike unless it has, within the previous sixty days, or any longer period that may be agreed to in writing by the trade union and the employer, held a secret ballot vote among the employees in the unit and received the approval of the majority of the employees who voted."

**Section 87.2: Lockout Vote**

An employers' organization must hold a secret ballot vote among the employers who are members of the organization and receive the approval of the majority of the employers who voted, unless a strike not prohibited by this Part has occurred.

"...an employer in the long-shoring industry, or other industry included in paragraph (a) of the definition in section 2, its employees and their bargaining agent shall continue to provide the services they normally provide to ensure the tie-up, let-go and loading of grain vessels at licensed terminal and transfer elevators, and the movement of the grain vessels in and out of a port."

This obligation is in addition to the requirement to continue providing services in the event of a strike or lockout, as stated in Section 87.4(1).
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public."

**Trade Union Obligations**

Trade unions are also required to continue providing services, operation of facilities, or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public.
"An employer or a trade union may, no later than fifteen days after notice to bargain collectively has been given, give notice to the other party specifying the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that, in its opinion, must be continued in the event of a strike or a lockout in order to comply with subsection (1) and the approximate number of employees in the bargaining unit that, in its opinion, would be required for that purpose."

Employees in the bargaining unit are required to continue providing services, operation of facilities, or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public.
"Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

**Board Role in Ensuring Public Safety and Health**

The Board plays a crucial role in ensuring public safety and health during a strike or lockout.
"Where the Board, on application pursuant to subsection (4) or referral pursuant to subsection (5), is of the opinion that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public, the Board, after providing the parties an opportunity to agree, may, by order, (a) designate the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public..."

The Board's order may also specify the manner and extent to which the employer, trade union, and employees must continue to provide services, operation of facilities, or production of goods.
"(b) specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation and production..."

question: What conditions must be met by an employer or a trade union before declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike?
answer:
**Section 89: Conditions for Declaring a Lockout or Authorizing a Strike**

**Section 89(1): Requirements for Declaring a Lockout or Authorizing a Strike**

No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part; (b) the employer and the trade union (i) have failed to bargain collectively within the period specified in paragraph 50(a), or (ii) have bargained collectively in accordance with section 50 but have failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement; (c) the Minister has (i) received a notice, given under section 71 by either party to the dispute, informing the Minister of the failure of the parties to enter into or revise a collective agreement, or (ii) taken action under subsection 72(2); (d) twenty-one days have elapsed after the date on which the Minister (i) notified the parties of the intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or to establish a conciliation board under subsection 72(1), (ii) notified the parties that a conciliation officer appointed under subsection 72(1) has reported, (iii) released a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a), or (iv) is deemed to have been reported to pursuant to subsection 75(2) or to have received the report pursuant to subsection 75(3); (e) the Board has determined any application made pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or any referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5); and (f) sections 87.2 and 87.3 have been complied with.

**Section 89(2): Requirements for an Employee to Participate in a Strike**

No employee shall participate in a strike unless (a) the employee is a member of a bargaining unit in respect of which a notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part; and (b) the requirements of subsection (1) have been met in respect of the bargaining unit of which the employee is a member.

**Section 87.2: Notice to Declare a Lockout or Authorize a Strike**

Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister.

**Section 87.3: Notice to Declare a Lockout or Authorize a Strike - Employer's Obligation**

Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister.

**Section 88.1: Strikes and Lockouts Prohibited During Term of Collective Agreement**

Strikes and lockouts are prohibited during the term of a collective agreement except if (a) a notice to bargain collectively has been given pursuant to a provision of this Part, other than subsection 49(1); and (b) the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met.

**Section 90 of the Canada Labour Code**

Section 90 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the circumstances under which the Governor in Council can intervene to defer a strike or lockout. According to this section, the Governor in Council may make an order deferring the strike or lockout during the period commencing on the day the order is made and ending on the twenty-first day following the date fixed for the return of the writs. This order may only be made during the time mentioned in subsection (1), which is
"...the time commencing on the date of a dissolution of Parliament and ending on the date fixed for the return of the writs at the next following general election and, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, adversely affects or would adversely affect the national interest..."
