question: What steps can an employee take if they believe their employer has taken action against them in contravention of subsection 247.98(4), and what is the role of the Head and the Board in handling the complaint?
answer:
**Complaint Handling Process**

**Step 1: Filing a Complaint**

An employee who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 247.98(4) may make a complaint in writing to the Head.
"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them: (a) the employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 173.01(5), 174.1(4) or 177.1(7) or of section 208, 209.3, 238, 239, 239.1 or 247.96..."

**Step 2: Notification of the Head**

The complaint shall be made to the Head not later than 90 days after the day on which the complainant knew, or in the Head’s opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint.
"Subject to subsection (3), the complaint shall be made to the Head not later than 90 days after the day on which the complainant knew, or in the Head’s opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint."

**Step 3: Investigation and Settlement**

The Head shall endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint.
"On receipt of a complaint made under subsection (1), the Head shall endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint."

**Step 4: Referral to the Board
"If a complaint is not settled under subsection (4) within the period that the Head considers to be reasonable in the circumstances, the Head must, on the written request of the employee who made the complaint that the complaint be referred to the Board, deliver to the Board the complaint made under subsection (1) and any other statements or documents that the Head has that relate to the complaint."

question: What actions can the Minister take to investigate employment in industrial establishments, and who can be appointed to carry out this investigation?
answer:
**Investigation Actions**

The Minister can take several actions to investigate employment in industrial establishments.
The Minister may
"...cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment..."(a)).

**Appointment of Investigators**

The Minister can appoint one or more persons to carry out the investigation.
A person appointed pursuant to subsection (1) has
"...all of the powers of a person appointed as a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act...", which includes the power to issue a summons and administer oaths.

**Powers of Investigators**

An investigator appointed by the Minister has the power to
"...issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry..."(a)).

**Staff and Remuneration**

The Minister can also engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the investigator in conducting the inquiry.
The Minister can "fix and pay their remuneration and expenses" (CLC-12.07(1.1)).

**Formal Inquiry Process**

In the event that a dispute or difference between an employer and employees exists or is apprehended, the Minister may appoint a commission to be designated as an Industrial Inquiry Commission.
The Commission shall
"...inquire into the matters referred to it by the Minister and endeavour to carry out its terms of reference..."

question: What powers does the Head have to gather information and conduct inspections under the Canada Labour Code, and who can assist or be delegated these powers?
answer:
**Powers of the Head**

The Head has the power to gather information and conduct inspections under the Canada Labour Code.
"The Head may (a) establish the form of notices of violation; (b) designate persons, or classes of persons, who are authorized to issue notices of violation; and (c) establish a short-form description for each violation to be used in notices of violation."

**Delegation of Powers**

The Head can delegate powers to other qualified individuals or classes of persons.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part."

**Assistance and Support**

The Head can be accompanied or assisted by other individuals during inspections.
"The Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and functions, be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary."

**Administrating Oaths and Statutory Declarations**

The Head has the power to administer oaths and statutory declarations.
"The Head may administer all oaths and take and receive all affidavits and statutory declarations required with respect to the Head’s powers set out in subsection 249(2) and certify to the administration, taking or receiving of them."

**Inspections and Examination of Records**

The Head has the power to inspect and examine records of employers, including books, payrolls, and other documents.
"For the purposes of this Part and the regulations, the Head may (a) inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee..."

**Right to Enter Premises**

The Head has the power to enter federal workplaces for the purpose of making inspections.
"The Head may, at any reasonable time, enter on any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business for the purpose of making an inspection authorized under subsection (2), and may, for that purpose, question any employee apart from his employer."

**Certificate of Authority**

The Head must furnish a certificate of authority to any person to whom powers are delegated.
"The Head shall furnish to every person to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated under subsection (1) a certificate of authority and, when entering any place used in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business the person, shall, when requested, show the certificate to the person in charge of that place."

question: What powers does the Head have in relation to administering oaths, taking affidavits, and receiving statutory declarations under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Powers of the Head**

**Administering Oaths and Receiving Statutory Declarations**

The Head has the power to
"...administer all oaths and take and receive all affidavits and statutory declarations required with respect to the Head’s powers set out in subsection 249(2)..."


**Delegation of Powers**

The Head may delegate their powers to "any qualified person or class of persons" subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister. This delegation is subject to the approval of the Minister, as stated in the document:
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part."

**Certificate of Authority**

The Head may provide a certificate of authority to delegated persons, which they must show when entering a federal workplace. This certificate is a symbol of the Head's authority and is required to be produced when exercising delegated powers.


**Limitation of Liability**

Delegated persons are not personally liable for their actions, as stated in the document:
"A person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection (2), is not personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the actual or purported exercise of..."

**Scope of Powers**

The Head's powers include the ability to
"...inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee..."(a)). This power is subject to the Head's discretion and is intended to ensure compliance with the Canada Labour Code.

question: What happens if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this impact potential prosecution?
answer:
**Failure to Pay Employee Wages**

**Section 251.04: Settlement of Amounts Due**

If an employer and an employee who has made a complaint relating to the non-payment of wages or other amounts to which they are entitled under this Part reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer
"...may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head." This section does not directly address the consequences of an employer's failure to pay an employee, but it does provide a mechanism for employers and employees to settle disputes and avoid prosecution.

**Section 251.14: Deposit of Moneys**

If the Head finds that an employer has failed to pay an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, the Head may determine the difference between the wages or other amounts actually paid to the employee and the wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled. The Head may then
"...employee and the wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled and the amount of that difference is agreed to in writing by the employee and his or her employer..."

**Consequences of Failure to Pay Employee Wages**

If the Head finds that an employer has failed to pay an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled, the employer may be required to pay the amount to the employee or to the Head. This can have significant consequences for the employer, as it may impact their ability to avoid prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to.

**Impact on Potential Prosecution**

No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head. This means that if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee wages or other amounts, they may be able to avoid prosecution if they can demonstrate that they have paid the amount to the employee or the Head.

question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices and records, and what information must be included in the report?
answer:
**Internal Audit Order**

The Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices and records
"...for the purpose of verifying compliance or preventing non-compliance with this Part..." This order must be made in writing, and the employer must provide a report of the results of the audit to the Head.

**Contents of the Order**

The order must specify the industrial establishment and class of employees to which it applies, the period of time to be covered by the internal audit, the provisions of this Part or the regulations with respect to which the internal audit was ordered, and the date by which the employer is to provide the report (CLC-251.001(2)). The report must also contain any information that the Head considers appropriate.

**Information to be Included in the Report**

The report must include information about the employer's non-compliance with any provision of this Part or the regulations (CLC-251.001(6)). If the employer determines that it had not complied with any provision, the report must set out the nature of the employer's non-compliance and the steps that have been or will be taken by the employer to comply with the provision. Additionally, if any wages or other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part are owed, the report must also state the name of the employee, the amount owed for the period of time covered by the internal audit, the method used to determine the amount owed, and any payment subsequently made to the employee with respect to that amount owed (CLC-251.001(7)).

**No False Information**

The employer must not make a false or misleading statement in a report (CLC-251.001(9)). The report must be accurate and truthful, providing a clear and detailed account of the employer's practices and records.

"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Head if they believe that the employer has contravened (a) any provision of this Part or of the regulations made under this Part; or (b) any order."

"A complaint under subsection (1) shall be made within the following period (a) in the case of a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, six months from the last day on which the employer was required to pay those wages or other amounts under this Part; and (b) in the case of any other complaint, six months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose."

"An employee shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under any of subsections 240(1), 246.1(1) and 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn."

question: Under what circumstances can the Head suspend consideration of a complaint made by an employee, and what are the requirements for the Head's decision to be implemented?
answer:
**Suspension of Complaint**

The Head may suspend consideration of a complaint made by an employee
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01..."

**Requirements for Suspension**

The Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice
"...the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures." [CLC-251.02(2)]

**End of Suspension**

The suspension ends when, in the Head's opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken. [CLC-251.02(4)]

**Implementation of Decision**

If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice the measures that the employee must take and the period of time within which the employee must take those measures. [CLC-251.02(2)]

**Extension of Time**

The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice. [CLC-251.02(3)]

**Decision to be Implemented**

The suspension ends when, in the Head's opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken. This means that the employee must take the specified measures within the specified period of time. [CLC-251.02(4)]

**No Right to Refuse Work**

If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the employee is no longer entitled to continue their refusal under subsection 128(15). [CLC-129(1.2)]

**No Right to Refuse Work**

The employee may continue to refuse, for the duration of the investigation, to use or operate the machine or thing, to work in the place or to perform the activity that may constitute a danger. [CLC-129(1.3)]

**No Right to Refuse Work**

On being informed of the Head's decision not to proceed with an investigation, the employee is no longer entitled to continue their refusal under subsection 128(15). [CLC-129(1.2)]

question: What happens when an employer and employee reach a settlement regarding non-payment of wages or other amounts under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this affect potential prosecution?
answer:
**Settlement of Amounts Due**

When an employer and employee reach a settlement regarding non-payment of wages or other amounts under the Canada Labour Code, the employer may pay the amounts to the employee or to the Head.
"If an employer pays the amounts to the Head, the Head must, without delay after receiving them, pay them over to the employee who is entitled to the amounts." **Effect on Potential Prosecution**

The settlement of amounts due has a significant impact on potential prosecution. According to the Canada Labour Code,
"No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head."

This quote emphasizes the importance of settlement and payment in preventing prosecution. By paying the amounts owed, the employer can avoid prosecution and ensure that the employee receives the wages or other amounts they are entitled to.

question: Under what conditions can the Head reject a complaint made under section 251.01, and what steps must be taken after a complaint is rejected?
answer:
**Conditions for Rejecting a Complaint**

The Head may reject a complaint made under section 251.01, in whole or in part, under the following conditions:
"...the subject-matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator..."

This condition indicates that the Head may reject a complaint if the issue has been resolved through a court or tribunal process.

**Grounds for Rejecting a Complaint**

The Head may reject a complaint if it is determined that the complaint is not within their jurisdiction, or if the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith. For example, a complaint regarding a third-party disclosing the results of an employee’s genetic test without consent may be rejected because the complainant cannot file this complaint with the Labour Program.

**Steps to be Taken After a Complaint is Rejected**

If a complaint is rejected, the employee must notify the Head in writing, with reasons, within 15 days after the day on which the employee is notified of the rejection. The employee may then request a review of the Head's decision, in writing, with reasons, within 15 days after the day on which the employee is notified of the rejection.

**Notice of Rejection of Complaint**

If a complaint has been rejected, the Head shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons, of the rejection. The employee shall be notified of the Head's decision, in writing, of the confirmation or rescission of the decision.

**Request for Review**

The employee may request a review of the Head's decision, in writing, with reasons, within 15 days after the day on which the employee is notified of the rejection. The Head may confirm the decision, or rescind it and re-examine the complaint.

If the Head concludes that the employer has not paid to the employee all wages and other amounts to which the employee is entitled under the Canada Labour Code for the period of six months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made, the Head must notify the employee in writing that their complaint is unfounded.
"If the Head deals with a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part, the Head must notify the employee in writing that their complaint is unfounded if the Head concludes that the employer has paid to the employee all wages and other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part for the period of six months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made."

question: What is the process for an employer or affected person to dispute a compliance order, payment order, or notice of unfounded complaint or voluntary compliance issued under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Process for Disputing a Compliance Order, Payment Order, or Notice**

**Before Filing a Complaint**

To dispute a compliance order, payment order, or notice of unfounded complaint or voluntary compliance issued under the Canada Labour Code, an employer or affected person must
"...send a written request with reasons to the Head for a review of the Head’s decision (a) subject to paragraph (b), within 15 days after the day on which the order or a copy of the order or the notice is served; or (b) if a compliance order is served with a notice of violation issued under subsection 276(1) for the same contravention, within 30 days after the day on which they are served."

**Eligibility and Timelines**

The request for review must be made within the specified timeframe, as stated in the Canada Labour Code:
"An employer or a director of a corporation is not permitted to request a review of a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the payment order and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the payment order in accordance with subsection 251.131(1), subject to, in the case of a director, the maximum amount of the director’s liability under section 251.18."

**Review Process**

If the request for review is made, the Head may
"...confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the payment order or the compliance order; or (b) confirm the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance, or rescind the notice, in which case the Head shall re-examine the complaint." The decision made by the Head may be served by personal service, registered mail, or any other means prescribed by regulation.

**Appeal Process**

If the employer or affected person is not satisfied with the review decision, they may request an appeal at the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). The request for appeal must be made within 15 days after the Labour Program review decision is served. The CIRB may only hear the appeal if it is based on a question of law or jurisdiction.

question: Who can appeal a decision made under subsection 251.101(3) of the Canada Labour Code, and what are the conditions for doing so?

**Appeal Process**

**Who Can Appeal a Decision?**

A person who is affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3) of the Canada Labour Code may appeal the decision to the Board, in writing, within 15 days after the day on which the decision is served.
"Subject to subsection (1.1), a person who is affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3), other than a decision to rescind a notice of unfounded complaint or a notice of voluntary compliance, may appeal the decision to the Board, in writing, within 15 days after the day on which the decision is served."

**Conditions for Appealing a Decision**

The person must meet the conditions outlined in subsection (1.1), which states that
"Only an employer to whom a compliance order has been issued may appeal a decision with respect to that order."

**Grounds for Appealing a Decision**

The request for appeal must contain a statement of the grounds of appeal.
"The request for appeal shall contain a statement of the grounds of appeal."

**Payment of Amount and Administrative Fee
"An employer or director of a corporation is not permitted to appeal a decision confirming or varying a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the decision — and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the decision in accordance with subsection 251.131(1) — less any amount and administrative fee paid under subsection 251.101(2)."

question: What are the responsibilities of the Head and the Board in terms of document provision and participation in an appeal under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Document Provision and Participation in an Appeal**

**Document Provision**

The Canada Labour Code outlines the responsibilities of the Head and the Board in terms of document provision and participation in an appeal.
The Head is required to provide documents to the Board upon request, as stated in Section 251.111(2):
"In an appeal under this Part, the Head shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed."

This quote highlights the importance of transparency and documentation in the appeal process. The Head is required to provide a copy of any document that was relied upon in making the decision, allowing the Board to fully understand the circumstances of the appeal.

**Participation in an Appeal**

The Board also has a responsibility to participate in an appeal, as stated in Section 251.111(5):
"The Head may, in an appeal under this Part, present evidence and make representations to the Board."

This quote emphasizes the role of the Head in presenting evidence and making representations to the Board. The Head is not only required to provide documents, but also to participate actively in the appeal process.

**Board's Responsibilities**

The Board is responsible for ensuring that the appeal process is fair and transparent. As stated in Section 251.111(4):
"The Board shall, on request of the Head, provide to the Head a copy of any document that is filed with the Board in the appeal."

This quote highlights the importance of communication and transparency in the appeal process. The Board is required to provide a copy of any document that is filed in the appeal, allowing the Head to stay informed and involved in the process.

**Head's Responsibilities**

The Head is responsible for ensuring that the appeal process is conducted in a fair and transparent manner. As stated in Section 251.111(1):
"The Board shall inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 251.11(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal."

This quote emphasizes the importance of notification and communication in the appeal process. The Board is required to inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought, providing a copy of the request for appeal.

question: What are the responsibilities of an employer in Canada regarding the provision and maintenance of employee work records and information as per the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Employer Responsibilities: Work Records and Information**

**Section 252: Information and Returns**

Every employer shall furnish any information that the Head may require that relate to their employees, including their wages, their hours of work and their general holidays, annual vacations and conditions of work as well as any returns that the Head may require.
"Marginal note: Records to be kept (2) Every employer shall make and keep for a period of at least 36 months after work is performed the records required to be kept by regulations made under paragraph 264(1)(a) and those records shall be available at all reasonable times for examination by the Head."

This quote highlights the employer's responsibility to keep and maintain employee work records for a period of at least 36 months. The records must be available for examination by the Head at all reasonable times.

**Section 125.1: Further Specific Duties of Employer**

Every employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls the activity, ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards.

This quote emphasizes the employer's responsibility to ensure the provision and maintenance of employee work records and information, including hazardous substances in the work place.

**Section 24: Keeping of Records**

Every employer shall make and keep a record in respect of each employee showing the date of commencement of employment and the date of termination of employment and shall keep such record for a period of at least 36 months after the date of termination of employment.

This quote highlights the employer's responsibility to keep and maintain employee work records, including the date of commencement and termination of employment.

question: How can the Head require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, and what are the implications of the methods used for serving notices?
answer:
**Methods of Serving Notices**

The Head may require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, and the methods used for serving notices are governed by Section 253 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Section 253: Notice to Furnish Information**

Where the Head is authorized to require a person to furnish information under this Part or the regulations, the Head may require the information to be furnished by a notice to that effect served by personal service, by registered mail addressed to the latest known address of the addressee, or by any other means prescribed by regulation, and that person (a)
"...if the notice is sent by registered mail, is deemed to have received the notice on the seventh day after the day on which it was mailed..." and (b)
"...shall furnish the information within such reasonable time as is specified in the notice."

**Implications of the Methods Used**

The method of serving notices has significant implications for the person receiving the notice. For example, if the notice is sent by registered mail, the person is deemed to have received the notice on the seventh day after the day on which it was mailed. This means that the person has a certain amount of time to respond to the notice and furnish the information requested.

**Proof of Service**

A certificate purporting to be signed by the Head certifying that a notice was sent by registered mail or by any other means prescribed by regulation to the addressee, accompanied by a true copy of the notice and by an identifying post office certificate of the registration or other proof, prescribed by regulation, that the notice has been sent or received, is admissible in evidence and is proof of the statements contained in the certificate, without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate.

**Statutory Instruments Act**

The Statutory Instruments Act does not apply in respect of notices referred to in subsection (1). This means that the rules governing the service of notices are specific to the Canada Labour Code and do not apply to other statutes.

**Registration and Proof of Service**

A certificate of the Head certifying that the information has not been furnished is admissible in evidence and in the absence of any evidence to the contrary is proof of the statements contained in it. This certificate is also evidence that the notice was sent or received, and that the information has not been furnished.

**Admissibility in Evidence**

A certificate under this section signed or purporting to be signed by the Head is admissible in evidence without proof of the Head's appointment or signature. This means that the certificate is considered evidence in a court of law, and its authenticity is not questioned.

**Methods of Serving Notices: Personal Service**

The Head may also serve notices personally, which means that the notice is delivered directly to the person receiving it. This method of serving notices is governed by Section 253 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Methods of Serving Notices: Registered Mail**

The Head may also serve notices by registered mail, which means that the notice is sent by postal mail and the person receiving it is deemed to have received it on the seventh day after it was mailed. This method of serving notices is also governed by Section 253 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Methods of Serving Notices: Other Means**

The Head may also serve notices by other means, such as facsimile or email, as long as the method of serving notices is prescribed by regulation. This means that the Head has the flexibility to choose the method of serving notices that is most effective in reaching the person receiving the notice.

question: What information must an employer provide to an employee in writing at the time of making a payment of wages?
answer:
**Canada Labour Code: Requirements for Payment of Wages**

**Section 254: Pay Statement Requirements**

An employer shall, at the time of making any payment of wages to an employee,
"...furnish the employee with a statement in writing setting out (a) the period for which the payment is made; (b) the number of hours for which the payment is made; (c) the rate of wages; (d) details of the deductions made from the wages; and (e) the actual sum being received by the employee."

**Section 254: Exemption from Requirements**

The Minister may, by order, exempt any employer from any or all of the requirements of subsection (1). However, this does not change the requirements that must be met by employers who are not exempt.

**Section 254: Details of Deductions**

The pay statement must also include "details of the deductions made from the wages". This information is crucial in understanding how much of the employee's wages are being deducted for various reasons, such as union dues or health insurance premiums.

**Section 254: Actual Sum Received by Employee**

The pay statement must also include "the actual sum being received by the employee". This information is essential in ensuring that the employee is aware of their exact wages and can plan their finances accordingly.

**Section 254: Period for Which Payment is Made**

The pay statement must also include "the period for which the payment is made". This information is necessary in understanding when the employee is entitled to payment of wages and can plan their finances accordingly.

**Section 254: Number of Hours for Which Payment is Made**

The pay statement must also include
"...the number of hours for which the payment is made..." This information is crucial in understanding the employee's work schedule and can help them plan their finances accordingly.

**Section 254: Rate of Wages**

The pay statement must also include "the rate of wages". This information is essential in understanding the employee's hourly wage and can help them plan their finances accordingly.

IPG-060_2:

{"id": "IPG-060_2", "type": "Interpretations, Policies and Guidelines", "title": "Deductions from wages or other amounts - IPG-060", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "WHEN A DEDUCTION IS FOUND TO HAVE BEEN AUTHORIZED IN WRITING PURSUANT TO PARAGRAPH 254.1(2)(C) OF THE CODE Subsection 254.1(1) prohibits an employer from making deductions from wages or other amounts except under specific circumstances as set out in subsection 254.1(2). One of these specific circumstances [paragraph 254.1(2)(c)] is when the deductions are "amounts authorized in writing by the employee". Paragraph 254.1(2)(c), "amounts authorized in writing by the employee", requires a written authorization by the employee consenting to the deduction of a specific amount. For every deduction made, the authorization must be in writing, specify a particular amount, and be given in a way that is truly consensual. Where it is found that the deduction of a particular amount has been authorized in writing by the employee, it must also be confirmed whether the authorization was truly consented to by the employee.  WHETHER THE TIMING OF THE AUTHORIZATION HAS AN IMPACT ON THE VALIDITY OF THE DEDUCTION General blanket authorizations in employment contracts, with or without specific amounts, may operate to assign responsibility or liability to the employee. However, the corresponding deduction requires a specific authorization. Whether the authorization for deduction is signed before, at the time of, or after the deduction is made is not a relevant factor on its own. A consent for wage deduction made at the time of or after an occurrence is more likely to be accepted than one which is made a considerable period before the deduction. The more specific and timely the authorization is to the actual occurrence the more likely it would be considered valid."

question: Under what conditions can an employer make deductions from an employee's wages or other amounts due to them?
answer:
**General Prohibition on Deductions**

An employer cannot make deductions from wages or other amounts due to an employee, except as permitted by or under section 254.1 of the Code.
"No employer shall make deductions from wages or other amounts due to an employee, except as permitted by or under this section."

**Specific Circumstances for Deductions**

The Code sets out specific circumstances under which an employer may make deductions from an employee's wages or other amounts. These circumstances include:
"...those required by a federal or provincial Act or regulations made thereunder..."
"...those authorized by a court order or a collective agreement or other document signed by a trade union on behalf of the employee..."
"...amounts authorized in writing by the employee overpayments of wages by the employer, and other amounts prescribed by regulation..."

**Authorization of Deductions**

In addition to the specific circumstances, an employer may also make deductions from an employee's wages or other amounts if the employee has authorized the deduction in writing.
"...amounts authorized in writing by the employee..."

**Timing of Authorization**

The timing of the authorization has an impact on its validity. A consent for wage deduction made at the time of or after an occurrence is more likely to be accepted than one which is made a considerable period before the deduction.
"A consent for wage deduction made at the time of or after an occurrence is more likely to be accepted than one which is made a considerable period before the deduction."

**Permitted Deductions**

The Code also sets out what constitutes a permitted deduction. These include deductions for damage to property, or loss of money or property, if any person other than the employee had access to the property or money in question.
"Notwithstanding paragraph (2)(c), no employer shall, pursuant to that paragraph, make a deduction in respect of damage to property, or loss of money or property, if any person other than the employee had access to the property or money in question."

**General Rule**

In general, an employer may only make deductions from an employee's wages or other amounts if the employee has authorized the deduction in writing, or if the deduction is required by a federal or provincial Act or regulations made thereunder.
"No employer shall make deductions from wages or other amounts due to an employee, except as permitted by or under this section."

**Consequences of Discrimination**

Every person who contravenes any provision of this Part or the regulations, other than a provision of Division IX, subsection 239.1(2), 239.2(1), 251.001(9) or 252(2) or any regulation made under section 227 or paragraph 264(1)(a) or (a.1); (b) contravenes any order made under this Part or the regulations; or (c) discharges, threatens to discharge or otherwise discriminates against a person because that person (i) has testified or is about to testify in any proceedings or inquiry taken or had under this Part, or (ii) has given any information to the Minister or the Head regarding the wages, hours of work, annual vacation or conditions of work of an employee.

question: What are the key considerations for instituting proceedings in respect of an offence under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART III - Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations and Holidays?
answer:
**Key Considerations for Instituting Proceedings**

**Time Limitation**

The key consideration for instituting proceedings in respect of an offence under this Part is the limitation period. According to Section 257 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Proceedings in respect of an offence under this Part may be instituted at any time within but not later than three years after the time when the subject-matter of the proceedings arose."

This quote highlights the importance of timing in instituting proceedings. The limitation period of three years is a crucial factor in determining when a complaint or information can be made under this Part.

**Minister's Consent**

Another key consideration is the requirement for the Minister's consent. According to Section 257 of the Canada Labour Code,
"No proceeding against a director of a corporation in respect of an offence under this Part shall be instituted except with the consent of the Minister."

This quote emphasizes the need for the Minister's approval before instituting proceedings against a director of a corporation. This provision ensures that the Minister is involved in the proceedings and provides a level of oversight.

**Procedure and Administration**

The key considerations for instituting proceedings in respect of an offence under this Part also involve the procedure and administration of the law. According to Section 251.01 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Head if they believe that the employer has contravened (a) any provision of this Part or of the regulations made under this Part..."

This quote highlights the importance of following the proper procedure for making a complaint. The employee must believe that the employer has contravened a provision of this Part or the regulations made under it, and must make the complaint in writing to the Head.

**Extension of Time**

In certain circumstances, the Head may extend the limitation period. According to Section 251.01 of the Canada Labour Code,
"The Head may, subject to the regulations, extend the period set out in subsection (2) (a) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made within that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint and that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority..."

This quote highlights the possibility of extending the limitation period in certain circumstances. The Head may extend the period if the complaint was made to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint, and if the person making the complaint believed that the official had that authority.

This quote emphasizes the potential consequence of conviction, where the employer may be required to pay compensation for loss of employment and reinstate the employee in their employ.

"An employer that fails to comply with an order of a convicting court made under section 258 is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and liable to a fine of not more than $1,000 for each day during which the failure continues."

**Purpose of the Governor in Council's Regulatory Power**

The Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 263 of the Canada Labour Code is aimed at
"...any regulations that the Governor in Council considers necessary respecting the establishment and operation of one or more pilot projects..."

**Establishment of Pilot Projects**

The Governor in Council has the authority to establish pilot projects for testing possible amendments to the Canada Labour Code, with the goal of "improving and better protecting employees' rights under this Part" (R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 263). These pilot projects can be established for
"...testing which possible amendments to this Part or the regulations made under this Part would improve and better protect employees’ rights under this Part..."

**Scope of Pilot Projects**

The Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 263 allows for the establishment of pilot projects for
"...any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province..." This includes corporations whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Regulatory Framework**

The Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 263 is subject to certain limitations. Regulations made under section 263 are repealed on the fifth anniversary of the day on which they come into force, unless they are repealed earlier (2018, c. 27, s. 504). This suggests that the Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 263 is intended to be temporary and limited in scope.

Every person or department that contravenes or fails to comply with a provision, direction, order or condition designated by regulations made under paragraph 270(1)(a) commits a violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations.

question: Who can be held liable for a violation committed by a corporation or a department under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Liability Under the Canada Labour Code**

**Who Can Be Held Liably?**

The Canada Labour Code outlines the liability for violations committed by corporations or departments. According to Section 274 of the Canada Labour Code,
"...any of the following persons who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the violation is a party to the violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations, whether or not the corporation or department has been proceeded against in accordance with this Part: (a) any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation; (b) any senior official in the department; or (c) any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department."

This quote highlights the specific individuals who can be held liable for violations committed by corporations or departments. The language used emphasizes the role of these individuals in directing or authorizing the violation, indicating that they are responsible for their actions.

**Officer, Director, Agent, or Mandatary**

The quote also mentions "any officer, director, agent or mandatary of the corporation" as a potential liable party. This phrase suggests that individuals in leadership or representative roles within the corporation can be held accountable for violations committed by the company.

**Senior Official in the Department**

Additionally, the quote mentions "any senior official in the department" as a potential liable party. This phrase highlights the importance of senior officials in departments in ensuring that violations are prevented or addressed.

**Other Persons with Managerial or Supervisory Functions**

The quote also mentions
"...any other person exercising managerial or supervisory functions in the corporation or department." as a potential liable party. This phrase emphasizes the importance of individuals in leadership or supervisory roles within the corporation or department in preventing or addressing violations.

question: What are the requirements for a notice of violation issued under the Canada Labour Code, and what information must it contain?
answer:
**Notice of Violation Requirements**

**Definition of Notice of Violation**

A notice of violation issued under the Canada Labour Code is a formal notification of a violation of the Code's provisions.
"If a person designated under paragraph 271(b) has reasonable grounds to believe that a person or a department has committed a violation, the designated person may issue a notice of violation..."

**Contents of Notice of Violation**

A notice of violation must contain specific information to ensure that the recipient is aware of the alleged violation and its consequences.
"The notice of violation shall (a) name the person or department that is believed to have committed the violation; (b) set out the relevant facts surrounding the violation; (c) set out the penalty for the violation; (d) inform the person or department of their right to contest the facts of the alleged violation or the penalty, by way of review and appeal, and of the procedure to be followed to exercise that right; (e) inform the person or department of the manner of paying the penalty set out in the notice; and (f) inform the person or department that, if they do not pay the penalty or exercise their right referred to in paragraph (d), they will be considered to have committed the violation and that they are liable for the penalty set out in the notice."

**Specific Requirements**

A notice of violation must be issued by a person designated under paragraph 271(b), and it must be served on the person or department believed to have committed the violation.
"If a person designated under paragraph 271(b) has reasonable grounds to believe that a person or a department has committed a violation, the designated person may issue a notice of violation..."

**Information to be Included**

A notice of violation must contain the name of the person or department believed to have committed the violation, the relevant facts surrounding the violation, the penalty for the violation, and information about the right to contest the facts or penalty.
"The notice of violation shall (a) name the person or department that is believed to have committed the violation; (b) set out the relevant facts surrounding the violation; (c) set out the penalty for the violation..."

**Consequences of Not Paying the Penalty**

A notice of violation must inform the person or department that they will be considered to have committed the violation and that they are liable for the penalty set out in the notice, if they do not pay the penalty or exercise their right to contest the facts or penalty.
"The notice of violation shall (a) name the person or department that is believed to have committed the violation; (b) set out the relevant facts surrounding the violation; (c) set out the penalty for the violation; (d) inform the person or department of their right to contest the facts of the alleged violation or the penalty, by way of review and appeal, and of the procedure to be followed to exercise that right; (e) inform the person or department of the manner of paying the penalty set out in the notice; and (f) inform the person or department that, if they do not pay the penalty or exercise their right referred to in paragraph (d), they will be considered to have committed the violation and that they are liable for the penalty set out in the notice."

question: Can a person or department named in a notice of violation under the Canada Labour Code claim defence based on due diligence or honest belief in certain facts?
answer:
**General Provisions**

**Defences Not Available**

A person or department named in a notice of violation does not have a defence by reason that the person or the department "...(a) exercised due diligence to prevent the violation..." or
"...reasonably and honestly believed in the existence of facts that, if true, would exonerate the person or the department." This is stated in Section 277(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

**Application of Common Law Principles**

Every rule and principle of the common law that renders any circumstance a justification or excuse in relation to a charge for an offence under Part II or III applies in respect of a violation to the extent that it is not inconsistent with this Part. This means that the common law principles that apply to other offences may also apply to violations under the Canada Labour Code.

**Presumption of Authenticity**

A document that appears to be a notice of violation issued under subsection 276(1) is presumed to be authentic and is proof of its contents in any proceeding in respect of a violation. This means that the person or department named in the notice of violation is presumed to have committed the violation, and the defence of due diligence or honest belief may not be claimed.

**Burden of Proof**

If the facts of a violation are reviewed or appealed, the person who issued the notice of violation shall establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the applicant or the appellant committed the violation. This means that the person or department named in the notice of violation must prove that they committed the violation, rather than the other way around.

**Proof of Violation**

It is sufficient proof of the violation to establish that it was committed by an employee or agent or mandatary of the person or of the department, whether or not the employee or agent or mandatary has been identified or proceeded against in accordance with this Part. This means that the person or department named in the notice of violation can be held liable for the violation, even if the employee or agent or mandatary who committed the violation has not been identified.

question: If a violation of the Canada Labour Code is committed and continues over several days, how is it treated under the code?
answer:
**Treatment of Continuing Violations**

**Section 278: Continuing Violation
"A violation that is committed or continued on more than one day constitutes a separate violation for each day on which it is committed or continued."

This quote from Section 278 indicates that a violation committed and continuing over several days is treated as a separate violation for each day it is committed or continued. This means that the violator is liable for multiple violations, each occurring on a different day.

**Section 279: Violation or Offence
"Proceeding with any act or omission as a violation under this Part precludes proceeding with it as an offence under Part II or III, and proceeding with it as an offence under Part II or III precludes proceeding with it as a violation under this Part."

This quote from Section 279 highlights the distinction between violations and offences under the Canada Labour Code. It states that a violation is not an offence, and therefore, section 126 of the Criminal Code does not apply in respect of a violation. This quote reinforces the idea that a continuing violation is treated as a separate violation for each day it is committed or continued.

**Section 280: Limitation Period
"No notice of violation in respect of a violation may be issued more than two years after the day on which the subject-matter of the violation arises."

This quote from Section 280 addresses the limitation period for issuing a notice of violation. It states that a notice of violation cannot be issued more than two years after the day on which the subject-matter of the violation arises. This quote provides context for the treatment of continuing violations, as it ensures that the violator is held accountable within a reasonable timeframe.

**Section 281: Liability
"Every person or department that contravenes or fails to comply with a provision, direction, order or condition designated by regulations made under paragraph 270(1)(a) commits a violation and is liable to a penalty of an amount to be determined in accordance with the regulations."

This quote from Section 281 provides insight into the liability of violators. It states that every person or department that contravenes or fails to comply with a provision of the Canada Labour Code commits a violation and is liable to a penalty. This quote reinforces the idea that a continuing violation is treated as a separate violation for each day it is committed or continued.

question: What is the effect of choosing to proceed with an act or omission as a violation under one part of the Canada Labour Code on the possibility of proceeding with it as an offence under another part?
answer:
**Effect of Proceeding with a Violation**

**Section 279: Violation or Offence**

Proceeding with any act or omission as a violation under this Part precludes proceeding with it as an offence under Part II or III, and proceeding with it as an offence under Part II or III precludes proceeding with it as a violation under this Part.

**Source: CLC-279, Section 279(1)**

This quote indicates that choosing to proceed with an act or omission as a violation under one part of the Canada Labour Code has a significant effect on the possibility of proceeding with it as an offence under another part.

**General Offences**

Every person who (a) being required to attend to give evidence pursuant to paragraph 16(a), fails, without valid excuse, to attend accordingly, (b) being commanded to produce, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), any document or thing in their possession or under their control, fails to produce the document or thing, (c) refuses to be sworn or to affirm, as the case may be, after being required to do so pursuant to paragraph 16(a), or (d) refuses to answer any proper question put to them, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), by the Board, a conciliation board, a conciliation commissioner, an arbitrator or an arbitration board, is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding four hundred dollars.

**Source: CLC-102, Section 102(1)(a)-(d)**

This quote highlights the consequences of choosing to proceed with an act or omission as a violation, indicating that it can lead to the loss of the possibility to proceed with it as an offence under another part.

**General Offences (Continued)**

Every employer or trade union who or that contravenes or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 50, 94 or 95 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars.

**Source: CLC-101, Section 101(2)**

This quote further emphasizes the effect of choosing to proceed with an act or omission as a violation, indicating that it can lead to the loss of the possibility to proceed with it as an offence under another part.

question: What is the procedure for a person or department to dispute a notice of violation under the Canada Labour Code, and what timeframe is allowed for making such a request?
answer:
**Procedure for Disputing a Notice of Violation**

**Request for Review**

A person or department that is served with a notice of violation may, within 30 days after the day on which the notice is served, or within any longer period that the Head allows,
"...make a request, in the manner prescribed by regulation, to the Head for a review of the penalty or the facts of the alleged violation, or both."

**Eligible Parties**

This procedure is available to "a person or a department" that is served with a notice of violation, indicating that the Canada Labour Code provides a framework for disputing notices of violation to both individuals and organizations.

**Timeframe for Making a Request**

The request for review must be made within 30 days after the day on which the notice is served, or within any longer period that the Head allows. This timeframe is specified in the Canada Labour Code, providing a clear understanding of when a person or department can dispute a notice of violation.

**Review Process**

Once a request for review is made, the Head will "examine the notice of violation and determine whether the penalty for the violation was determined in accordance with the regulations" (CLC-281). This review process aims to ensure that the penalty imposed is fair and reasonable, providing a mechanism for disputing the notice of violation.

**Cancellation or Variation of Notice**

If the Head determines that the facts of the alleged violation are not as set out in the notice, or that the penalty for the violation was not determined in accordance with the regulations, the Head shall cancel or vary the notice of violation (CLC-281). This outcome provides a positive result for the person or department that made the request for review, indicating that the notice of violation was unfounded.

question: What happens when an appeal is made regarding a penalty for a violation under the Canada Labour Code, and what are the possible outcomes of this appeal process?
answer:
**Appeal Process Under the Canada Labour Code**

**Grounds of Appeal**

When an appeal is made regarding a penalty for a violation under the Canada Labour Code, the request for appeal must contain a "statement of the grounds of appeal" (CLC-285(2)). This statement should clearly outline the reasons why the appellant believes the penalty was incorrect or that the violation did not occur.

**Decision of the Board**

If the appellant submits a request for appeal, the Board shall determine, as the case may be, whether the amount of the penalty for the violation was determined in accordance with the regulations or whether the appellant committed the violation, or both (CLC-287(1)). The Board's decision is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court.

**Possible Outcomes of the Appeal Process**

If the Board determines that the amount of the penalty for the violation was not determined in accordance with the regulations, the Board shall "correct the amount of the penalty" (CLC-287(2)). This means that the penalty will be adjusted to reflect the correct amount. If the Board determines that the appellant committed the violation, the appellant is liable for the penalty that is set out in the decision.

**Payment of Penalties**

If the Board determines that the appellant committed the violation, the appellant is liable for the penalty that is set out in the decision. The employer must comply with the order as soon as possible, or within the time period ordered by the referee (CLC-287(5)). This means that the employer must pay the penalty to the employee or return the payment to the employer.

**No Review by Certiorari, etc.
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this section." This means that the appeal process is separate from the regular court system, and the Board's decisions are final and binding.

The Governor in Council has the authority to make regulations for testing possible amendments to improve compliance with certain parts of the Act.

**Section 161: Pilot Projects**

The Governor in Council may make any regulations that the Governor in Council considers necessary respecting the establishment and operation of one or more pilot projects for testing which possible amendments to this Part or the regulations made under this Part would improve the prevention of accidents, injuries and illnesses arising out of, linked with or occurring in the course of employment to which this Part applies, including regulations respecting the manner in which and the extent to which any provision of this Part or the regulations made under this Part applies to a pilot project, and adapting any such provision for the purposes of that application.
